topic: Browser context sharing authority versus capture-chip revoke/send races
research_questions: How do browser permission and screen/tab capture systems define authority, consent, indicators, revocation, and send-time validation?
What TOCTOU or revoke/send races are addressed by browser standards and platform security guidance?
Which UI and protocol patterns make capture scope, current authority, and revocation state legible to users?
How should Puppet Master bind browser context sharing, capture chips, revocation, and audit evidence?

sources.title: Screen Capture
sources.material_relevance: Defines getDisplayMedia surface choice, display-capture permission state, permissions policy, privacy indicators, source-scope controls, and capture feedback requirements.

sources.title: Permissions
sources.material_relevance: Defines permission keys, lifetimes, expiry, revocation algorithms, and the required synchronization work after a user revokes permission.

sources.title: Media Capture and Streams
sources.material_relevance: Defines MediaStreamTrack live/ended lifecycle, end events, source stopping, permission-driven track termination, and the privacy-indicator effect of stopping capture tracks.

sources.title: Capture Handle - Bootstrapping Collaboration when Screensharing
sources.material_relevance: Specifies opt-in browser-context identity sharing, permitted-origin filtering, current-handle reads, and change events for captured applications.

sources.title: Privacy-preserving screen sharing controls
sources.material_relevance: Documents Chrome controls for excluding monitors or the current tab, exposing user-initiated tab switching, and avoiding app-directed selection of a specific window.

sources.title: docs/media/capture
sources.material_relevance: Maps Chromium capture UX to implementation surfaces: target chooser, screen-capture indicator, and tab indicator/switcher with stop and switch actions.

sources.title: WebRTC Security Architecture
sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) RFC Editor
sources.material_relevance: Requires explicit consent, separate screen-sharing consent, no JS-installed permanent screen grants, and unambiguous indicators with a way to terminate capture.

sources.title: Security Considerations for WebRTC
sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) RFC Editor
sources.material_relevance: Analyzes oversharing, browser-context confidentiality, higher consent needs for screens, peer identity, and the distinction between capture consent and transmission consent.

sources.title: ScreenCast - XDG Desktop Portal documentation
sources.material_relevance: Documents portal-owned source selection, explicit persistence modes, single-use restore tokens, withdrawal fallback, closed sessions, and non-reused PipeWire stream serials.

sources.title: Screen capture - Windows apps
sources.material_relevance: Shows secure system picking, explicit user consent, a system yellow border around each active capture item, and reuse of a consented item across sessions.

sources.title: ScreenCaptureKit
sources.material_relevance: Documents requesting screen-recording permission before capture and platform cancellation/error states that an implementation must surface and handle.

sources.title: CWE-367: Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition (4.20)
sources.material_relevance: Defines the check/use state-change race, its unauthorized-resource consequences, and the design guidance to avoid relying on a stale pre-use check.

findings.claim: The Screen Capture specification requires the user agent to let the end user choose the display surface on every getDisplayMedia request; application constraints may influence presentation but cannot narrow the user's choice and are applied after selection.
findings.notes: This is normative W3C text. The current publication is a Working Draft, so it is a strong standards signal rather than a claim that every browser has identical behavior.

findings.claim: Display capture is modeled as an express powerful feature whose permission state is prompt or denied, not a persisted granted state; the specification also binds it to a self permissions-policy allowlist and live display-source indicators.
findings.notes: The source explicitly says granted must not be used for display-capture and that live indicators distinguish display kinds even though there is one permission descriptor.

findings.claim: The Permissions specification treats authority as time-bounded state: expiry resets the state and queues revocation work for associated browsing contexts, while explicit revocation runs the feature revocation algorithm and removes the permission-store entry.
findings.notes: The standard separates permission-store state from the feature-specific revocation algorithm, which is directly relevant to synchronizing active capture and send pipelines.

findings.claim: MediaStreamTrack has live and ended states; when a source ends for a reason other than an explicit stop, the user agent sets readyState to ended, notifies the source, and fires ended, while explicitly stopping capture tracks can affect privacy indicators.
findings.notes: The lifecycle rules are general, while the cited permission-rescind example is written for camera and microphone. The Screen Capture specification separately extends the privacy-indicator model to display capture.

findings.claim: Capture Handle is an opt-in authority boundary: a captured application chooses whether to expose an origin and handle, limits visibility by permitted origins, and causes capturing applications to receive a change event when the observable handle changes.
findings.notes: The draft makes captured-side consent and capturing-side observation explicit; it does not grant the capturing application unrestricted cross-origin inspection.

findings.claim: Chrome's documented privacy controls let the application exclude entire monitors or the current tab and request a browser-level tab-switch control, but Chrome intentionally does not let the application preselect a specific window or screen.
findings.notes: This pattern keeps high-risk source choice in browser-owned UX while allowing an application to express broad safety preferences.

findings.claim: Browser and platform patterns make capture status independently visible and controllable: Chromium documents a screen indicator and a tab indicator/switcher with stop or switch actions, Windows draws a yellow border around each active item, and RFC 8827 requires an unambiguous indicator and separate screen-sharing consent.
findings.notes: The exact visual treatment is platform-specific, but independent visibility and user termination are consistent requirements or implementation patterns.

findings.claim: WebRTC security guidance distinguishes consent to access local capture from consent to transmit data and notes that browser-enforced identity covers the party controlling media, not every downstream recipient to whom that party may forward it.
findings.notes: This makes a single boolean such as capture_granted insufficient as a complete send authorization record.

findings.claim: The XDG ScreenCast portal separates source selection from start, supports explicit non-persistent or revocable persistence modes, uses single-use restore tokens, falls back to prompting when sources or stored permissions are unavailable, and warns that reusable PipeWire node IDs can misidentify streams while serials are not reused.
findings.notes: This is a concrete mature open-source platform contract for session identity, restoration, source lifecycle, and revocation-sensitive selection.

findings.claim: MITRE CWE-367 describes a TOCTOU weakness as checking a resource property and then using the resource after the property can change; consequences include unauthorized resource access and actions that occur in an unexpected state.
findings.notes: The capture-chip race is an application-specific instance of this general check/use hazard, not a claim that CWE-367 itself specifies browser capture.

findings.claim: A revoke/send race should be treated as a session-authority problem rather than solved by a cached permission read: each send or attach operation should be bound to a revocable capture session and revalidated at the commit/use point.
findings.notes: This is a synthesis of permission revocation, track lifecycle, TOCTOU, and separate transmission-consent guidance; none of the sources defines Puppet Master's exact send protocol.

findings.claim: No reviewed public source defines a Puppet Master-specific atomic contract that ties browser context identity, capture-chip state, revocation, send authorization, and audit evidence together.
findings.notes: This is a bounded no-evidence result for the reviewed source set, not proof that no such contract exists elsewhere.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Browser-owned surface selection with application safety hints: the user chooses the tab, window, or monitor, while application preferences only shape presentation or exclude broad risky classes.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Represent source choice as a user-owned authority grant and retain the chosen scope as evidence; do not treat an application-selected path as equivalent consent.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Independent capture visibility and termination: browser or OS UI exposes the active capture and supplies stop or switch controls outside the captured page's normal DOM.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: The capture chip should be an observable state projection with a direct revoke path, not the sole authority or a decorative status label.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Captured-context identity is opt-in, origin-filtered, and change-notified through Capture Handle rather than inferred from pixels or unrestricted cross-origin access.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Use an explicit context witness and permitted-origin policy for collaboration, and treat handle changes as state transitions.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Platform portal persistence is explicit and revocable: sessions can be non-persistent, app-lifetime, or until explicitly revoked; restore tokens are single-use and invalid stored permissions fall back to a new prompt.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Any restore or reuse capability needs a bounded lifetime, source scope, revocation check, and token generation rather than blind replay.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Capture consent and recipient or peer consent are distinct security decisions; a trusted application can still forward media to a party the browser cannot independently enforce.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Keep source authority, recipient identity, and active send authorization as separate fields and state transitions.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Session identity uses a non-reused generation or serial when the underlying resource identifier may be recycled.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Bind every send and receipt to a capture-session generation, not only to a browser tab ID, stream label, or OS node ID.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Across browser and platform examples, the convergent architecture is a system-owned capture authority and indicator combined with application-owned session semantics and evidence.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Use a two-layer state model: authoritative capture lifecycle from the browser or OS, plus a Puppet Master send and audit state that cannot outlive it.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: No reviewed standard establishes a universal cross-platform named capture-chip protocol or atomic revoke/send primitive.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: The missing cross-platform contract must be explicitly designed and verified per browser and OS rather than assumed from one platform's indicator behavior.

failure_modes.failure_mode: The user believes a window or tab is shared but a broader application or monitor is captured, exposing unrelated windows, notifications, or cross-origin content.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Preserve the browser or OS picker, display the exact selected surface and surface type, exclude the current tab or monitor where appropriate, and require scope confirmation for high-risk surfaces.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A page or send pipeline keeps treating a capture as authorized after the user or platform has revoked or ended it.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Make revocation and track-ended signals terminal for the affected session, stop or detach all dependent sinks, and invalidate any queued send work.

failure_modes.failure_mode: The implementation checks capture authority, then a revoke or scope change occurs before the frame or stream is attached to the network sink.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Use a commit-time authority gate with a session generation or epoch; reject sends whose ticket no longer matches the authoritative capture session.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A stale cached context handle is used after the captured application changes its permitted identity or handle configuration.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Subscribe to capturehandlechange, reread the current handle at each authority-sensitive operation, and treat a changed witness as a possible scope or recipient reauthorization event.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A recycled platform stream identifier is mistaken for the previously authorized source after destruction, hotplug, resolution change, or resume.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Bind the session to a non-reused serial or generation and verify the source scope before reconnecting or restoring.

failure_modes.failure_mode: The indicator is hidden, ambiguous, or lacks a user-controlled stop path, so the user cannot tell what is live or cannot revoke it independently of page code.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Keep system or browser indicators visible and actionable, mirror scope and state in the application chip, and test that page code cannot suppress the termination path.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A restore token or long-lived capture permission is replayed after the source disappeared or the user withdrew permission.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Use single-use or expiring restore credentials, verify source availability and current permission at restore, and prompt again when either is invalid.

failure_modes.failure_mode: No reviewed source proves that one generic capture chip can reach every browser and OS revocation surface and cancel every already-queued send.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Treat cross-platform propagation and queued-frame behavior as an explicit test gap; require a browser/OS matrix and observable negative receipts before claiming closure.

implications.implication: For the assigned feature refs, model capture authority as a revocable session with explicit source scope, captured-context identity, lifetime, indicator state, generation, and revocation state.
implications.rationale: The sources expose these dimensions separately; the proposed session object is a Puppet Master synthesis that makes their relationships auditable.

implications.implication: A capture-chip revoke must invalidate sends at the commit/use boundary, not merely update rendered chip state or a cached permission value.
implications.rationale: Permission revocation is asynchronous feature work and TOCTOU arises when the check is separated from use; a commit gate closes that race window.

implications.implication: The application should record source authority and network-recipient authority independently, with a send decision that requires both current capture authority and current recipient authorization.
implications.rationale: WebRTC guidance explicitly separates local capture consent from communications consent and notes that application identity does not guarantee the final downstream recipient.

implications.implication: Revocation should be monotonic and idempotent: increment the session generation, stop or detach dependent tracks and sinks, cancel queued sends, and emit one auditable terminal decision even if browser, OS, and chip events race.
implications.rationale: The sources provide revocation, ended-state, session-close, and race guidance; monotonic/idempotent handling is the proposed integration rule.

implications.implication: A context-handle change should be visible to the send authorization layer and may require reauthorization when the captured origin or handle witness changes.
implications.rationale: Capture Handle defines current reads and change events but does not specify Puppet Master's send semantics; treating a changed witness as an authority-sensitive event is a conservative product inference.

implications.implication: The evidence record should distinguish user-selected source scope, current capture session generation, indicator state, revocation reason, recipient identity, and final send outcome.
implications.rationale: Those sources distinguish source scope, identity, persistence, indicators, and recipient concerns; the proposed fields prevent a single granted bit from obscuring a race.

implications.implication: The reviewed sources provide no evidence that the supplied OPF feature refs alone specify a complete cross-platform atomic revoke/send and audit contract; research should inform, but not close, that implementation assurance claim.
implications.rationale: The source set contains standards and platform patterns, not Puppet Master canonical implementation acceptance criteria.

novel_ideas.idea: Use an authority lease plus a one-shot send ticket: the lease carries session_id, generation, source scope, captured-context witness, and expiry; a send ticket is accepted only when its generation still matches the authoritative lease at commit time.
novel_ideas.rationale: This combines permission lifetime, changeable capture identity, and TOCTOU avoidance into a concrete protocol shape; it is not defined by any cited source.

novel_ideas.idea: Implement a two-signal revocation latch in which browser or platform lifecycle events and the application-chip revoke action both increment the same session generation and converge on one idempotent stop path.
novel_ideas.rationale: The sources show multiple independent lifecycle and indicator authorities; a shared latch is a proposed race-resistant integration mechanism.

novel_ideas.idea: Treat Capture Handle as a context witness rather than a permission grant: require an opt-in, permitted-origin handle to be current at authority-sensitive operations, and never infer context authority from pixels alone.
novel_ideas.rationale: The handle draft supplies explicit identity signaling while WebRTC security guidance describes the risk of screen-derived cross-origin information; the separation is a proposed design rule.

novel_ideas.idea: Expose a scope ladder that mirrors browser and platform surfaces—tab, window, monitor—with progressively stronger user acknowledgement for broader scopes and an always-visible current-scope chip.
novel_ideas.rationale: The sources identify surface classes, monitor leakage risk, and oversharing; the ladder is a proposed UX treatment.

novel_ideas.idea: Create a capability-lineage receipt that records the user-selected scope, session serial or generation, context witness version, indicator state, revocation epoch, recipient identity, and the final send commit decision.
novel_ideas.rationale: It makes the authority lineage and race outcome inspectable; no cited source defines this receipt format.

novel_ideas.idea: Define a platform-adapter conformance matrix for revoke propagation, indicator termination, track-ended timing, restore-token invalidation, and already-queued-frame behavior before accepting a cross-platform atomicity claim.
novel_ideas.rationale: No reviewed source provides a universal adapter or test contract for all target browsers and operating systems; this is a proposed verification need.

unresolved_questions.question: Which browser and OS signals are authoritative for display-capture revocation when a platform can expose track ended, mute, indicator, or session-close signals with different timing?
Can each supported browser and OS provide a reliable send-time authority check, or must Puppet Master enforce the check only through an application-owned session gateway?
When a Capture Handle changes during an active share, should the current send be revoked, paused for reauthorization, or continue with updated context metadata?
What indicator and stop affordances are available and testable for each intended native, web, and WASM deployment, and which one is the authoritative user-visible status?
After local revocation, what is the required treatment of frames already buffered, encoded, handed to a peer, or queued in a transport, and what evidence proves that treatment?
Which minimum receipt fields are sufficient to prove that the source selected by the user, the source live at commit time, and the scope actually sent were the same authority generation?
